questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: How does an object-store key differ from a file-system path?
options: Its slashes are a prefix convention rather than real parent directories
Its characters are restricted to a fixed alphabet chosen by the bucket
It addresses a mutable byte stream that writers can extend in place
It carries a directory entry that a rename updates atomically in one step

questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: What is the normal way to change the contents of an object?
options: Open the object and edit the bytes at a chosen offset in place
Write a complete new object, usually under a new versioned key name
Append the changed rows directly to the end of its Parquet footer
Rename the containing prefix so the old key resolves elsewhere

questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: Why is object-store rename often expensive and non-atomic?
options: Keys are immutable once written, so a rename must fail on every attempt
Objects carry no checksum, so a rename cannot verify the copied bytes
It is usually a full copy to the new key followed by deleting the old
Listing lags behind writes, so the renamed key stays invisible for hours

questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: Why is a manifest better than inferring a table from a prefix listing?
options: A manifest compresses the data columns it references into one object
A manifest replaces per-object permissions with a single bucket policy
A manifest makes the referenced data objects mutable and appendable
A manifest names the exact committed files with their sizes and stats

questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: A batch eventually writes 1000 objects and a reader lists during execution. What can the reader legitimately observe?
options: Only the objects written so far, such as 400 of the eventual 1000
All 1000 keys immediately, because listing waits for the batch to end
A half-written byte range inside one of the already completed objects
No keys at all until the writer renames the staging prefix into place

questions.topic: Object Stores vs File Systems: Immutability and Listing
questions.question: Why are immutable segments plus later compaction preferable to repeatedly appending one object?
options: Object stores cannot serve byte ranges, so segments must stay small
Replacing a growing object amplifies writes and races other writers
Immutable objects cannot be cached, so segments keep caches correct
Compaction runs only on a mounted file system with real directories

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: What does single-object atomic publication guarantee?
options: That a group of puts and deletes becomes visible as one transaction
That a prefix listing returns the same key set to every later reader
That a reader never observes a half-written version of that whole object
That deletes of related objects all take effect at the same instant

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: Why does strong per-key consistency not provide a table transaction?
options: Because reads of a newly written key can still return the previous bytes
Because objects hold only bytes and cannot carry any table schema
Because every write to a bucket is eventually consistent by design
Because many puts and deletes still become visible at different times

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: What prevents two writers from silently overwriting the same snapshot pointer?
options: A conditional write that succeeds only if the pointer still matches
A larger pointer object, so a partial overwrite becomes easier to detect
A deeper prefix hierarchy that isolates each writer's pointer copy
A list request issued after every row so writers can see each other

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: How should files A and B be replaced by C without exposing missing or duplicate rows?
options: Delete A and B first, then upload C into the same partition prefix
Write C first, then commit metadata that drops both A and B and adds C
Overwrite A's bytes with C's contents and leave B in place unchanged
Publish a prefix listing taken after C lands as the new commit record

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: A client times out during a conditional pointer update. What should it do before retrying?
options: Delete every object it wrote so the retry starts from a clean prefix
Assume the commit failed, since a timeout is reported before any write
Read the pointer to learn whether the commit actually took effect
Overwrite the pointer unconditionally to make the outcome deterministic

questions.topic: Consistency and Atomicity Limits of Object Storage
questions.question: Why should garbage collection traverse retained manifests instead of trusting the latest prefix contents?
options: Because manifests list only metadata objects and never any data objects
Because a prefix always holds exactly the files of the newest commit
Because listing order proves the sequence in which commits were made
Because retained snapshots and orphans share prefixes with live files
